analysis.one_liner: Taxes employers whose workers earn low wages, unless they provide health and retirement benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in January 2019 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge large employers an escalating excise tax when many of their workers earn under about 218% of the federal poverty line (roughly $27,000 a year). The tax starts at a quarter of the employer's total wage bill and climbs with the share of low-wage workers, but drops 25 points if the employer offers decent health coverage and a real retirement plan to those workers. Government and churches are exempt. The bill was introduced by Sen. Sherrod Brown, sent to the Finance Committee, and never acted on.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers at large companies — fast-food, retail, warehouse, and hospitality employees earning under roughly $27,000 a year — would benefit two ways: their employers would have a strong financial reason to raise pay above the threshold or provide health coverage and employer-funded retirement contributions, and the tax revenue would fund federal programs. Workers who got employer health plans and pension contributions would gain directly.

how_it_helps.text: Employers must pay an excise tax of 25% to 100% of their total wage bill, scaled to how many of their workers earn less than 218% of the federal poverty line, giving them a powerful incentive to raise pay or add benefits [S3].

The tax is cut by 25 percentage points for employers that offer full-time low-wage workers health coverage covering at least 60% of costs at an affordable employee share, plus an employer-funded retirement plan contributing at least 5% of pay [S3].
The low-wage threshold is pegged to the federal poverty line, so the pressure to raise wages adjusts automatically as living costs rise [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large and mid-size employers with many low-paid workers — chain restaurants, retailers, hotels, warehouses, and staffing firms — would bear the tax, and the cost would show up either as higher wages and benefits for workers or as reduced hiring and profits. Employers that pay low wages and offer no benefits would pay the most.

drawbacks.text: The penalty is extremely steep: an employer where more than 75% of workers are low-wage would owe a tax equal to 100% of its entire wage bill, a scale that could force layoffs, cut hours, or push firms to replace employees with contractors rather than raise pay [S3].
The tax applies to all wages the employer pays, not just the low-wage portion, so a company with a mixed workforce could face a large bill even if most of its workers are reasonably paid [S3].

The 180-day payroll-deposit trigger would sweep in many ordinary mid-sized and smaller businesses alongside the big chains the bill targets, and the compliance burden of tracking employee income against a poverty-line threshold each year would fall on all of them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — making profitable companies pay for the health care and public assistance their low-wage workers end up needing — is real, and the benefit offset is a genuine nudge toward health and retirement coverage. But the design is blunt: a tax that can reach 100% of an employer's total wage bill is so steep that honest critics would expect it to push work toward contractors and part-time arrangements before it raises wages. A more targeted version would tax only the wages of low-wage workers rather than the firm's whole payroll.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on January 24, 2019, joined by Sen. Dick Durbin, the only cosponsor [S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which was the last action it ever received [S5].
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill for the remaining two years of the 116th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large low-wage employers — fast-food, retail, and warehouse chains — came out ahead, since they never faced the new tax or the pressure to raise pay or add benefits. The low-wage workers the bill aimed to help gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Corporate Freeloader Fee Act to tax employers with many low-wage workers.

for.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or vote on the bill after it was referred to the Finance Committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only two supporters were Democrats and no vote was ever held, so the chamber's partisan split never got a chance to show itself.

industries.industry: Large low-wage employers (fast food, retail, hospitality, warehouses, staffing)
industries.note: These firms would face an excise tax of 25% to 100% of their wage bill unless they raise pay above roughly $27,000 a year or provide health and retirement benefits. The bill died in committee, so they kept the status quo, where taxpayers and public assistance fill the gap left by low pay.

Employers would get a tax discount for offering low-wage workers coverage meeting minimum-value standards, creating a new pool of employer-sponsored customers. Workers would get coverage at an affordable share of pay.

industries.industry: Retirement plan providers and asset managers
industries.note: The bill requires employer contributions of at least 5% of pay for low-wage workers to earn the tax discount, steering new retirement assets into workplace plans that these firms administer.
